records.text: Any recurrent neural network (RNN) is effectively a very deep network.
The depth of an RNN equals the input sequence length.
As activations and gradients propagate through time in an RNN, we repeatedly multiply by the same weight matrix W.
If the spectral radius of W is less than 1, the gradients shrink exponentially (vanishing gradients).
If the spectral radius of W is greater than 1, the gradients explode.
Exploding gradients cause numerical overflows and obvious failure.
Vanishing gradients are far more dangerous than exploding gradients.
With vanishing gradients, the loss still decreases.
Gradients with respect to W do not vanish because W participates in the most recent steps.
The network still trains, yet it makes its decisions based only on the last few elements of the sequence.
The network loses the ability to have long-term memory.
To give the gradient a shortcut past the repeated multiplications, we introduce a constant error carousel.
The constant error carousel is exactly the same idea as residual connections in ResNet.
This was pioneered in the 1990s (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1995/1997; Gers & Schmidhuber, 2000).
This gave rise to the most important recurrent unit.
An LSTM maintains two separate vectors: the cell state c_t (the “highway” for long-term memory) and the hidden state h_t (the normal working memory).
The whole LSTM cell is organized around gates.
Gates are tiny linear classifiers that output a vector of values in (0,1) via a sigmoid and act as a control signal, deciding what to erase, write, or read.
The candidate cell state is computed as c'_t = \tanh(W_{xc}x_t + W_{hc}h_{t-1} + b_{c'}).
The input gate is computed as i_t = \sigma(W_{xi}x_t + W_{hi}h_{t-1} + b_i).
The forget gate is computed as f_t = \sigma(W_{xf}x_t + W_{hf}h_{t-1} + b_f).
The output gate is computed as o_t = \sigma(W_{xo}x_t + W_{ho}h_{t-1} + b_o).
The new cell state is computed as c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t.
The new hidden state is computed as h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t).
The forget gate f_t multiplies the old cell state element-wise: values near 1 “keep”, near 0 “erase”.
The candidate c'_t proposes new numbers to write.
The input gate i_t selects which parts of c'_t are actually written.
Because the forget gate already erased the corresponding cells, writing is simply addition.
The output gate o_t decides which parts of the updated cell state should be exposed to the next hidden state (and used by the rest of the network).
Crucially, when the forget gate is fully open (f_t → 1), we obtain c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t.
Hence, ∂c_t/∂c_{t-1} = 1, which provides the constant error carousel.
The constant error carousel is a highway for gradients that is only interrupted when we explicitly choose to erase.
LSTM has many weight matrices (eight in the vanilla version, up to eleven with peepholes).
LSTM requires large memory sizes (d ≥ 256 typically).
LSTM is expensive to train.
Only around 2015 did sufficient compute become available to train huge LSTMs.
Yet LSTM still stands – modern recurrent systems (e.g. AlphaStar) consistently prefer LSTM over other recurrent units.
A known issue is that the gates only see h_{t-1}, which is o_{t-1} \odot \tanh(c_{t-1}).
If the output gate is closed, the gates have no direct information about the cell state.
The fix is to add direct peepholes – extra weight matrices that multiply c_{t-1} in the gate equations.
With peepholes, the input gate becomes i_t = \sigma(W_{xi}x_t + W_{hi}h_{t-1} + W_{pi}c_{t-1} + b_i).
The forget gate becomes f_t = \sigma(W_{xf}x_t + W_{hf}h_{t-1} + W_{pf}c_{t-1} + b_f).
The output gate becomes o_t = \sigma(W_{xo}x_t + W_{ho}h_{t-1} + W_{po}c_{t-1} + b_o).
Many LSTM variations exist.
The survey “LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey” (Greff et al., 2015) showed that you can even remove an entire gate without much performance loss.
The GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) was developed by Cho et al. (2014).
The GRU simplifies LSTM while preserving the error carousel.
There is no separate cell state in GRU; everything is in the hidden state h_t.
Instead of separate forget and input gates, a single update gate u_t produces a convex combination of the old state and a candidate.
The update gate is computed as u_t = \sigma(W_{xu}x_t + W_{hu}h_{t-1} + b_u).
The reset gate is computed as r_t = \sigma(W_{xr}x_t + W_{hr}h_{t-1} + b_r).
The candidate hidden state is computed as h'_t = \tanh(W_{xh'}x_t + W_{hh'}(r_t \odot h_{t-1})).
The new hidden state is computed as h_t = (1 - u_t) \odot h'_t + u_t \odot h_{t-1}.
u_t close to 1 keeps the old memory; u_t close to 0 replaces it with the candidate.
The reset gate r_t selects which parts of the previous state to use when computing the candidate.
GRU has only 6 weight matrices (vs. 8 for vanilla LSTM, 11 with peepholes).
In 2015–2016 NLP papers almost universally adopted GRU because it is more efficient.
Today, large-scale practice has switched back to LSTM for reasons that are mostly empirical: LSTM seems to scale better to truly hard problems.
Take-away: Both LSTM and GRU implement the constant error carousel, enabling gradient flow through arbitrarily long sequences.
LSTM remains the gold standard for large recurrent networks.
Neurobiologically, attention is as fundamental as memory and cognition (A.R. Luria).
Attention acts as a filter between a very short-term working memory (a few seconds) and further processing.

Crucially, unlike a convolutional network that processes every pixel equally, humans can completely miss objects in their field of view if attention is directed elsewhere (the famous “invisible gorilla” experiment).
Human vision is structured around foveal glimpses.
In foveal glimpses, high resolution is only at the centre of gaze; the rest is blurry.
The brain stitches these glimpses together by rapid saccadic eye movements.

The original motivation for attention in neural networks was to mimic this efficiency: look at a few small, high-resolution patches of a large image, choose where to look next, and make a decision, thus drastically reducing input size.
Early works (Mnih et al., 2014; Ba et al., 2015) used an RNN to select a sequence of glimpse locations.
At each step, g_t = f_g(\mathbf{x}_t, l_{t-1}).
l_t is sampled from a distribution p(\cdot \mid f_l(h_t)).
a_t is sampled from a distribution p(\cdot \mid f_a(h_t)).
The network received a reward only at the end (e.g. correct classification), so training was done with reinforcement learning (e.g. REINFORCE).
Later models like DRAW used variational inference.
These models are now outdated, but they established the principle of looking at parts of the input sequentially.
The real breakthrough came by applying attention to encoder–decoder sequence‑to‑sequence models.
A standard RNN encoder compresses the entire input sentence into a single vector z.
For short sentences this works, but: if z is too small, it cannot hold enough information for long inputs.
If z is made very large, the decoder LSTM becomes gigantic and requires quadratic numbers of weights that cannot be trained.
As a result, quality is good for short sentences and collapses for long ones.
The solution is to produce a representation for every input token and let the decoder reweigh them at each step.
A bidirectional encoder produces a vector z_i for every input token i.
At decoder step t (hidden state s_{t-1}), an attention network a scores each input position: e_{t j} = a(s_{t-1}, z_j).
Softmax turns the scores into a convex combination: \alpha_{t j} = \operatorname{softmax}(e_{t1}, e_{t2}, \dots).
The context vector is the weighted sum: c_t = \sum_j \alpha_{t j} z_j.
The decoder now uses c_t along with the previous output y_{t-1} and its hidden state to produce the next token.
The attention network is tiny – typically around 2% of the total parameters – yet it drives the results.
The attention network is never explicitly supervised (we don’t know which source word aligns to which target word).
The whole model is trained end‑to‑end on parallel sentences.
The attention weights emerge as meaningful alignments.

Interpretable attention matrices are a hallmark of this approach: for translation, they usually form a diagonal, with off‑diagonal spikes for reordered words or multi‑word phrases (e.g. French “la destruction” → English “destruction”).
Around 2015‑2016, Google Translate switched to such an architecture.
This switch caused a phase transition in translation quality.
The translation became good enough that post‑editing was faster than translating from scratch.
The same attention idea works for images: instead of compressing a CNN’s output into a single vector, we keep a 14×14 feature map and compute attention over these spatial locations.
The caption generator can then look at different parts of the image while generating each word (e.g. “woman”, “throwing”, “frisbee”).
Hard attention (sampling a single location) and soft attention (convex combination) were both explored (Xu et al., 2015).
Vaswani et al. (2017) proposed the Transformer architecture, built entirely on attention, discarding recurrence.
The original paper modestly aimed for comparable performance with higher efficiency.
The transformer turned out to be extremely general and scalable.
The transformer now underlies nearly all state‑of‑the‑art models.
The transformer is an encoder–decoder design for machine translation.
The encoder consists of 6 identical layers, each containing a self‑attention sublayer and a feed‑forward sublayer, with residual connections and layer normalization.
The decoder consists of 6 identical layers, each containing a masked self‑attention, an encoder–decoder attention, and a feed‑forward sublayer (again with residuals and layer norm).
Input tokens are first passed through a learned embedding layer, becoming vectors.
The whole transformer operates on sequences of vectors, rewriting them into context‑aware representations.
The decoder is autoregressive: it generates one token at a time.
A final linear + softmax layer produces output token probabilities.
In neural search, documents and queries are encoded into a shared latent space, and relevance is measured by the dot product.
Self-attention applies this idea to the same set of vectors: each input vector is simultaneously the query and a “document”.
From an input sequence X = [x_1, ..., x_L] (each x_i \in \mathbb{R}^D) we compute three projections.
Queries Q are computed as Q = X W_Q, where W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times d_k}.
Keys K are computed as K = X W_K, where W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times d_k}.
Values V are computed as V = X W_V, where W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times d_v}.
Queries Q and keys K live in the same space (dimension d_k).
Values V can have a different dimension d_v (often d_v = d_k).
The attention weights are computed as scaled dot-products: \operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V.
Dot products Q K^T yield a matrix of raw affinities between every query and every key.
Scaling by \sqrt{d_k} prevents the dot products from growing too large.
With random vectors, the variance of the dot product is approximately d_k.
Without scaling, the softmax would saturate into one‑hot vectors, losing gradient signal.
Softmax converts each row into a convex combination.
Multiplying by V produces the output as a weighted sum of the value vectors.
Every output position is directly connected to every input position in a single step – the path length is 1, regardless of distance in the sequence.
This is a huge advantage over RNNs.
The cost is a quadratic complexity O(L^2) in the sequence length.
This quadratic complexity is the central computational challenge of transformers.
A single attention head projects the input into a small space (d_k \approx 64), which is too small to capture all relevant relationships.
Instead, we run H independent heads in parallel, each with its own W_Q^{(h)}, W_K^{(h)}, W_V^{(h)}.
MultiHead(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \dots, \text{head}_H) W_O, where \text{head}_h = \operatorname{Attention}(X W_Q^{(h)}, X W_K^{(h)}, X W_V^{(h)}).
W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{H d_v \times D} projects the concatenated result back to the model dimension D.
This gives the model multiple “ways of looking” at the data and mixes the different perspectives.
The Transformer decoder is trained to predict the next token given the prefix.
For efficiency, the whole output sequence is fed to the Transformer decoder at once during training.
During training, future tokens must not influence the prediction of the current token.
Causal masking zeros out the softmax inputs for future positions, setting the attention weights for those positions to zero.
The encoder-decoder attention mechanism in the Transformer is a cross-attention layer.
In the encoder-decoder attention, the queries come from the decoder’s previous layer, which represents the tokens produced so far.
In the encoder-decoder attention, the keys and values come from the encoder’s output, which is the full source representation.
The encoder-decoder attention is essentially the same self-attention mechanism, but with Q, K, V originating from two different sequences.
The attention matrix resulting from encoder-decoder attention is not square.
Encoder-decoder attention gives the decoder a direct window into the source.
Using full words as tokens would require a vocabulary of millions, including typos and inflected forms.
Using characters as tokens would make sequences too long.
Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) is a deterministic Huffman-coding procedure that builds a subword vocabulary.
The BPE procedure starts with individual characters as the initial vocabulary.
In BPE, all adjacent pairs of tokens in the corpus are counted.
In BPE, the most frequent pair of tokens is replaced with a new token (for example, ‘a’ + ‘t’ becomes ‘Z’).
BPE repeats the steps of counting pairs and replacing the most frequent pair until the desired vocabulary size is reached.
In BPE, common morphemes such as '-ed' and '-tion' become single tokens, while rare words stay as multiple subword tokens.
Because the self-attention layer treats the input as an unordered set, position information must be injected.

In the original Transformer, sinusoidal positional encodings are defined as \(PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\) and \(PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\), where \(pos\) is the position and \(i\) is the dimension index.
Different dimensions of the sinusoidal positional encodings oscillate at different frequencies, mimicking a positional numeral system in a continuous way.
The dot product of two sinusoidal positional encodings depends only on their relative distance \(i-j\).
Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE) treat the embedding vector in pairs \((x_{2k}, x_{2k+1})\) as 2D vectors.

In RoPE, each pair is transformed by applying a rotation matrix: \(\begin{pmatrix} x'_{2k} \\ x'_{2k+1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(k\theta) & -\sin(k\theta) \\ \sin(k\theta) & \cos(k\theta) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_{2k} \\ x_{2k+1} \end{pmatrix}\).
Because rotations add (\(k\theta + l\theta = (k+l)\theta\)), the dot product between two RoPE-encoded vectors depends only on the offset \(k-l\), giving a perfect distance-preserving arithmetic.
Transformers replace recurrence with self-attention.
Self-attention in Transformers achieves direct connections between all positions.
Self-attention in Transformers enables massive parallelisation.
Transformers scale far better than LSTMs.
Doubling the number of parameters in Transformers reliably improves performance.
Transformers underlie modern Large Language Models (LLMs) with trillions of parameters.
The main weakness of Transformers is the quadratic \(O(L^2)\) complexity in sequence length.
The quadratic \(O(L^2)\) complexity of Transformers in sequence length has motivated an entire field of efficient attention variants.
